scenes.caption: A specific story about this customer can make you ignore what usually happens.
Base-rate neglect: focusing on one case's details and underweighting how common that outcome is overall.
Illustrative, schematic bars: if most offline cases in your history are power or SIM issues, check those first.
Start with the base rate, then adjust for case-specific evidence, such as a firmware signature in the logs.
Chesterton's reformer finds a fence across a road and wants it cleared because he sees no use for it.
The wiser reply: go and find out why it was put up, and then you may remove it.
Treat it as a short investigation, not a veto: who added the rule, what incident prompted it, does the cause still exist?
If the reason is gone, remove the rule, ideally as a reversible trial. If nobody knows why, time-box an experiment.
The map is not the territory: any model, report or metric is a simplified picture of the thing itself.
The CSAT score, the SLA report and the ticket status are maps. The customer's actual experience is the territory.
Illustrative: an escalation shows 'In progress with engineering' for nine days. The status was set on day one; nobody touched it since.
Pick one dashboard number and trace three underlying cases by hand to see what the number hides.
Inversion solves problems backwards: instead of asking how to achieve a goal, ask what would guarantee failure.
To ruin escalations: send them without logs, let cases sit unwatched, change priority silently, close before the fix is confirmed.
The list of failures becomes a checklist of things to prevent.
Avoiding every failure does not by itself create success, so pair inversion with a picture of what good looks like.
Parkinson's 1955 line: work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.
Illustrative: a report 'due Friday' gets done Friday afternoon. Asked for by Wednesday noon, it takes the same two hours and is no worse.
Tighter deadlines suit tasks with slack. For complex or creative work, rushing creates rework.
It began as satire about bureaucracy, not a study. Treat it as a hypothesis and set deadlines from a realistic estimate.
Myth: Eisenhower designed the four-box grid. Reality: it was popularised later, notably by Stephen Covey in 1989.
The tool is still useful: sort work into urgent and important, important only, urgent only, and neither.
Illustrative, schematic bars: urgent pings filled the week; coaching and root-cause work got no time at all.
Give most attention to important work before it becomes urgent. A famous name on a tool is not evidence that it works.
Most escalation delays are caused by what is missing, not by what is wrong.
Every clarifying question bounces the case back through the queue and can add a day to resolution.
A good escalation answers up front: what the customer sees, identifiers, what was tried, scope and impact, the ask and deadline.
Illustrative: 'device offline, please check' takes three round trips; a complete escalation can be picked up immediately.
A common mistake at shift change: passing on a status, 'waiting on engineering', instead of the state of the situation.
State means what was tried, what is suspected, what the customer was told, what is due next and who is committed to it.
Illustrative: the note said only 'engineering looking'. Night shift never knew about the 9 pm update promise, so the customer escalated.
Hand over explicitly: the incoming person is told, and acknowledges, that they now own it.
Once a customer problem is traced to a product defect, a hand-off happens. Who owns the customer now?
One view: support owns the customer until they confirm resolution. The other: once engineering accepts the case, they own it.
Agreed: the customer needs one clear voice, engineers need uninterrupted time, and unclear ownership creates gaps.
Evidence is balanced. Editorial view: engineering owns the fix; support owns customer updates on a fixed schedule.
Any process wobbles: some weeks have more tickets, some fewer, with no real cause. Schematic line, not data.
Shewhart's 1931 control charts draw limits around the process average to separate routine variation from genuine signals.
Illustrative: weeks run 18 to 30. A week of 31 prompts a review that finds nothing; a steady rise to 40 is spotted late.
Know your normal range and write signal rules in advance. Look for runs and trends, not just single outliers.
Feedback without a case in hand is an opinion the agent can argue with.
It moves from 'you are slow on escalations' to 'on this case the log request came on day three; what made that hard?'
Read cases in full, ask what they were thinking before offering your view, and agree one behaviour to try on the next case.
Sampling only struggling agents feels like surveillance. Sample everyone, include strong work, keep reviews apart from scoring.
The question is not 'can AI do it' but 'what happens when it is wrong, and who will notice?'
Score each task on two things: the cost of an error, and checkability, whether a person can verify it quickly against a source.
Cheap and checkable: automate. Cheap, hard to check: spot audits. Costly, checkable: AI drafts, human approves. Costly, hidden: human-led.
Pilot only on low-cost, easy-to-check tasks, then revisit the scoring as data comes in: measured error rates beat gut feel.
Psychological safety: the shared belief it is safe to ask and admit uncertainty. Applying it to escalations is an interpretation.
Low safety: agents hold cases too long, or escalate in a panic. High safety: they escalate early, with clear context.
Illustrative: an agent sits on a case for four days after a colleague was criticised for escalating. The customer complains twice.
Your reaction shapes it: thank someone publicly for an early escalation, even one that turned out to be unnecessary.
The five whys: when a problem occurs, ask why repeatedly until you reach a cause you can act on.
Ohno's own example traces a stopped machine back through several causes to a missing strainer, not simply a blown fuse.
It follows one chain, so different people reach different roots, and it can stop at a convenient answer like 'human error'.
Branch the chain: at each why, write every plausible cause, then test each causal link with evidence, not agreement.
